title: Polyglot Inference Adapter — prototype notes (Triton/TensorRT/custom-op)
content:
Context:

We need a pragmatic prototype that lets the serving runtime load and orchestrate multiple execution backends (Triton-managed models, TensorRT-serialized engines, and a simple custom-kernel path) under a single routing and KV-cache semantics. The goal is to exercise integration tradeoffs before we commit to a final API surface for the kernel/adapter layer. This doc captures the prototype architecture, experiment artifacts, measured tradeoffs, and open questions.

Goals (short):
- Prove an adapter shim that normalizes inference lifecycle across Triton, TensorRT, and custom-kernel invocation.
- Evaluate latency and memory behavior when switching engines mid-sequence (fallbacks / rollbacks).
- Validate KV cache consistency across heterogeneous backends and the overhead of cache materialization/serialization.
- Surface scheduling interactions when engines have incompatible batching semantics.

Non-goals: full production-ready robustness; final API. This is explicitly hacky to iterate quickly.

High-level prototype architecture (notes):
- Adapter shim abstraction (polyglot-adapter): lightweight Rust shim sitting between request router and backend pool. Responsibilities:
  - translate runtime request (token-level attention context + metadata) -> backend-specific call (Triton gRPC, TRT C++ call, custom CUDA kernel invocation)
  - manage per-request KV cache handles and a thin incarnation id to track cache validity across model versions/engine variants
  - expose capability flags (supports-batched-prefix, supports-streaming-kv, supports-quantized-weights)
- Backend implementations (prototype):
  - triton-backend: sends requests to Triton with a small boxed protobuf payload; uses Triton’s CUDA buffers for inputs/outputs
  - tensorrt-backend: uses serialized engine lib via a tiny C++ bridge + JNI-like FFI wrapper; supports int8/16/32 paths depending on engine
  - custom-backend: a simple cuBLAS/cuDNN custom-op path compiled as a plugin; used for exploring alternate attention kernels and kv-cache layout
- Runtime pouch: each adapter instance owns a GPU context + small pinned host buffer pool for fast transfers. Adapter instances are placed in a per-node pool and registered with the scheduler.

KV-cache model used for prototype:
- Core invariant: a single logical KV cache per logical model-version and request sequence. The adapter returns a stable KV reference token to the runtime to represent the cached state.
- Implementation: KV cache stored in host pinned memory as the canonical copy. Backends receive either:
  - a pointer to a GPU-resident snapshot (when warmed), or
  - the host copy and let the backend materialize to its engine-specific layout (materialize-on-demand).
- Eviction policy (prototype): LRU per adapter instance with size caps + an async writeback to a per-node spill file when > 2x cap.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Models: 7B transformer (baseline), small LSTM-attn toy (for microkernel tests)
- Backends tried: Triton (latest 24.11 with CUDA 12.2), TensorRT 9.2 serialized engines (fp16, int8), custom kernel (hand-tuned fused attention)
- Workloads: single-token completion, long-chained generation (prefix length 1024, gen length 512), many short parallel requests (N=64)
- Scheduling modes: eager-assign (dedicated adapter instance per request stream), pooled-assign (adapter instance pooled and shared), affinity-assign (pin by model-version + warm cache affinity)

Key microbench results (summary; numbers are median across 100 runs on p4d.24xlarge-like node):
- Single-token cold (no kv warm):
  - Triton: 14.2 ms
  - TensorRT (fp16 engine): 9.8 ms
  - Custom fused kernel: 8.6 ms
- Single-token hot (kv materialized on GPU):
  - Triton: 6.1 ms
  - TensorRT: 4.7 ms
  - Custom: 4.1 ms
- Long-sequence throughput (per-token latency averaged across 512-step gen with prefix 1024):
  - Triton: 9.8 ms
  - TensorRT: 7.0 ms
  - Custom: 6.5 ms
- Parallel short requests (N=64 concurrent single-token hot): tail-95 latency:
  - Triton pooled: 180 ms (queueing + worker startup)
  - TensorRT pooled: 110 ms
  - Custom pooled: 95 ms

Observations and practical tradeoffs:
1) Triton integration simplicity vs performance variance:
   - Pros: Fast to onboard models, standardized gRPC/HTTP surface, automatic memory mgmt on server-side. Great for teams that want operational simplicity.

   - Cons: Layered RPC + shared server scheduling adds observable tail latency under bursty small-request workloads. Triton’s model server-level batching/granularity makes low-latency single-token cases worse unless you run one model per server instance (costly).

2) TensorRT engines give predictable token latency but increase complexity around quantization/engine tuning and model-variant explosion. Serialized engines are fragile across minor CUDA/cudnn/TensorRT changes — we had to reserialize engines for driver upgrades in labs.

3) Custom kernel path achieves best per-token latency (particularly for fused attention + KV layout tuned for our runtime), but the maintenance surface is high (we implement attention, rotary, kv layout, rotary scaling, etc.). This path is best for tight SLA customers or experimental kernels.

4) KV cache placement: host-canonical + materialize-on-demand is simplest for correctness, but materialization cost can blow up cold-latency. Keeping warm GPU-resident caches and affinity scheduling yields the best steady-state latency.

5) Scheduling semantics mismatch: Triton expects larger batches to amortize RPC overhead. TensorRT and custom can do tiny micro-batches efficiently. A scheduler that is backend-aware (and can use distinct batching windows per adapter) lowers tail latency by ~25% in our tests.

6) Memory fragmentation and pinned buffers: adapter-local pinned pools reduce transfer overheads but make total memory accounting less predictable. We saw OOM risk if pooled pinned buffers were not reclaimed aggressively; adding soft-limits + periodic compaction reduced OOM repairs by 60%.

Detailed experiment notes (how we ran things):
- TensorRT FFI bridge: simple C++ wrapper exposing "engine_infer(int session_id, float* input, int input_len, float* output, void* kv_handle)". We serialized a minimal FFI and used cbindgen + Rust FFI in the adapter. Heap pinning must be explicit.
- Triton harness: spin up a per-node Triton container with multiple models loaded; we used HTTP synchronous requests in prototype to simplify instrumentation. We disabled Triton’s internal batching to compare raw performance.
- Custom kernel build: single-file CUDA fused_attention.cu compiled with nvcc flags -O3 -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80. Exposed the same FFI as TRT to keep adapter translation minimal.

Open questions (prioritized):
- KV cache serialization format: should we standardize on a small cross-backend proto for quick snapshot/transfer? Tradeoff: serialization CPU cost vs clarity/cross-compatibility.
- How much of the adapter's responsibilities should be moved into the runtime vs into backend-specific drivers? E.g., should materialization be in adapter or in runtime cache manager?
- Operator experience: what debugging surface do we provide when an adapter fails materialization mid-request? Circuit-breakers + graceful fallback to lower-quality models need concrete flow docs.
- Can we build a small "micro-engine" verifier that can run translated weights (a subset of ops) to validate engines post-serialization automatically?

Practical recommendations for next-phase design based on prototype:
- Define a minimal adapter interface: capability flags + three operations: InitSession, InferSync, MaterializeKV. Keep it tiny and stable.
- Scheduler needs backend-aware batching windows. Implement a small policy layer: per-backend target_batch_size, max_latency_ms, and affinity score for warm caches.
- Keep host-canonical KV store but add a fast-path for GPU-resident cached snapshot references. Provide a small documented snapshot proto.
- For Triton-heavy customers, recommend dedicated model servers (1:1) for low-latency workloads or accept higher tail latency and use Triton-exclusive autoscaling tiers.
- Invest in a nightly engine-reserialize test matrix for TensorRT to catch ABI fragility early.

Action items / next experiments:
- A1: Implement serialization proto for KV snapshots (Li) — prototype + perf test for serialize/deserialize CPU cost (due 2025-02-05).
- A2: Scheduler policy: add per-backend batching windows and measure tail-95 on mixed synthetic workload (Miguel) — due 2025-02-12.
- A3: Build a tiny engine verifier that loads TRT engine and runs a single-reference forward against the runtime CPU reference (Samir) — WIP.
- A4: Add instrumentation for pinned-buffer usage and implement compaction trigger in adapter (Anya) — due 2025-02-18.

Quick checklist for reviewers:
- Does the adapter interface capture the right minimal ops? (InitSession / InferSync / MaterializeKV)
- Are the capability flags sufficient to express backend differences? (backends currently report supports-batched-prefix, supports-streaming-kv, supports-quantized-weights)
- Are we comfortable with host-canonical KV cache + materialize-on-demand as the default?

Notes to self / stray thoughts:
- Could try a hybrid approach where Triton runs a minimal execution engine that calls our custom fused kernels via a C++ plugin — keeps Triton operationality but fixes tail latency. Worth a spike.
- Consider a compact bitmask version of KV snapshot for fast transfers (avoid copying entire tensor if only lexical prefixes change).

Appendix: commands / how to reproduce a microbench locally (prototype hacks)
- start triton: docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 -v $PWD/models:/models nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.11 tritonserver --model-repository=/models
- run triton microbench: python tools/triton_microbench.py --model small-transformer --mode single_token --n 100
- build custom kernel: nvcc -O3 fused_attention.cu -o fused_attention.so --shared -Xcompiler "-fPIC"
- run tensorrt bridge test: ./trt_bridge --load engine.plan --input sample.npz --kv /tmp/kv_snapshot.bin

If you want, I can extract the adapter interface sketch into a small open PR and wire up a minimal unit test harness that runs the three backend mocks and asserts stable KV semantics.

-- Anya
